lead: Divisibility is the arithmetic of remainders: a divides b when b = a·k for some integer k. Primes are the integers that cannot be split this way, and every integer is built from them. The greatest common divisor measures what two integers share; the Euclidean algorithm finds it by repeated division instead of factoring. These ideas sit behind fraction reduction, error-checking codes, RSA keys and hashing. The core results are the basic divisibility rules, the infinitude of primes, and gcd(252,105) by hand and by the extended algorithm.
prereq: You need: basic integer arithmetic and proof by contradiction (see Unit 1, Proof methods: direct, indirect and by contradiction).

blocks.text: For integers a and b, write a|b (read “a divides b”) when b = a·k for some integer k. Here a is a divisor of b, and b is a multiple of a. For example, 3|12 because 12 = 3·4, while 5∤12. For a ≠ 0, a|0 because 0 = a·0. Do not confuse a|b with the fraction a/b.

items: If a|b and b|c, then a|c. Proof: b = ak and c = bm, so c = a(km).
If a|b and a|c, then a|(bx + cy) for all integers x and y. Proof: b = ak and c = al, so bx + cy = a(kx + ly).
If a|b, then a|bc for every integer c. Proof: if b = ak, then bc = a(kc), so a|bc.
If a|b and b|a with a and b nonzero, then a = ±b. Proof: b = ak and a = bl, so a = a(kl); hence kl = 1, so k = l = 1 or k = l = −1.

sections.h3: Primes, unique factorization and counting primes

blocks.text: A prime is an integer p > 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and p. A composite is an integer n > 1 that is not prime. The number 1 is neither prime nor composite. The only even prime is 2.

The fundamental theorem of arithmetic says every integer n > 1 has a prime factorization n = p₁<sup>e₁</sup>p₂<sup>e₂</sup>…pᵣ<sup>eᵣ</sup>, with primes pᵢ and positive integer exponents eᵢ. The factorization is unique up to the order of the factors. For example, 252 = 2²·3²·7 and 105 = 3·5·7.

Suppose there are finitely many primes p₁, p₂, …, pₖ. Let N = p₁p₂…pₖ + 1. N > 1. Each pᵢ divides the product p₁p₂…pₖ, so pᵢ does not divide N, because N leaves remainder 1 on division by pᵢ. Thus N has no prime factor from the list. But N is either prime itself or has a prime factor. Either way there is a prime outside the list, contradicting the assumption. Hence infinitely many primes exist.

Let π(n) be the number of primes ≤ n. The prime number theorem states π(n) ~ n/ln n; the ratio π(n)/(n/ln n) tends to 1 as n grows. Here ln is the natural logarithm. For n = 10, π(10) = 4 (the primes 2, 3, 5, 7), close to 10/ln 10 ≈ 4.34.

For integers a and b, not both zero, gcd(a,b) is the largest positive integer d with d|a and d|b. For nonzero integers a and b, lcm(a,b) is the smallest positive integer m with a|m and b|m. Example: gcd(252,105) = 21 and lcm(252,105) = 1260. Note that lcm(0,b) is not defined, which is why the product formula is restricted to nonzero a and b.

Prime factorization gives both values at once. Write each integer as a product of prime powers, using exponent 0 for a prime that is missing. For each prime p, let α be its exponent in a and β its exponent in b. Then gcd uses p<sup>min(α,β)</sup> and lcm uses p<sup>max(α,β)</sup>.

blocks.where: a and b are nonzero integers; |ab| is the absolute value of their product.

blocks.text: Why: for each prime p, the exponents min(α,β) and max(α,β) add to α + β. The product on the left therefore has the same prime exponents as |ab|. This formula fails if one number is zero, so use it for nonzero integers. For 252 = 2²·3²·7 and 105 = 3·5·7: gcd = 3·7 = 21; lcm = 2²·3²·5·7 = 1260.

sections.h3: Euclidean algorithm, extended algorithm and Bezout

blocks.text: The division algorithm says that for an integer a and an integer b > 0, there are unique integers q and r with a = qb + r and 0 ≤ r < b. Here q is the quotient and r is the remainder. If b > 0, then gcd(a,b) = gcd(b,r).

Reason: any common divisor of a and b divides r = a − qb, so it divides b and r. Conversely, any common divisor of b and r divides a = qb + r, so it divides a and b. The two pairs have exactly the same common divisors, hence the same gcd.

Repeat the division with (b,r) until the remainder is 0. The remainders strictly decrease: r < b, then the next remainder is less than r, and so on. The process must stop. The last nonzero remainder is gcd(a,b). This is the Euclidean algorithm; some syllabi call it the repeated-division method.

The extended Euclidean algorithm also back-substitutes each remainder as a combination of the previous two numbers. It produces integers x and y with ax + by = gcd(a,b). Bezout's theorem states that such integers x and y always exist for integers a and b not both zero. The next chapter, modular arithmetic, uses this to invert numbers modulo n.

figure.caption: The last non-zero remainder is 21, and back substitution gives 21 = (−2)·252 + 5·105.

spec.title: Euclidean algorithm for gcd(252,105)
spec.aria: Repeated division reduces 252 and 105 to gcd 21, then back substitution writes 21 as −2·252 + 5·105.

examples.question: Use the Euclidean algorithm to find gcd(252,105). Then write 21 as a linear combination of 252 and 105, and verify the combination.
steps: The last nonzero remainder is 21, so gcd(252,105) = 21.
examples.check:
def egcd(a, b):
    if b == 0:
        return a, 1, 0
    g, x1, y1 = egcd(b, a % b)
    return g, y1, x1 - (a // b) * y1

g, x, y = egcd(252, 105)
print(g)
print(x)
print(y)

traps: Stopping at the first remainder instead of continuing to remainder 0. The gcd is the last nonzero remainder, not the first.
Calling 1 a prime. By definition a prime must exceed 1; 1 is neither prime nor composite.
Sign errors in back substitution. Check the final Bezout form by substituting the numbers.
Using gcd(a,b)·lcm(a,b) = ab without absolute value or with zero; use |ab| and nonzero a,b.
Swapping min and max exponents: gcd takes the smaller exponent, lcm takes the larger.

quiz.q: Define a|b for integers a and b.
quiz.a: a|b means b = ak for some integer k; a is a divisor of b.

quiz.q: Is 1 a prime? Give the definition reason.
quiz.a: No. A prime p must satisfy p > 1; 1 does not.

quiz.q: State the fundamental theorem of arithmetic and factor 252 into primes.
quiz.a: Every integer n > 1 is a product of primes uniquely up to order; 252 = 2²·3²·7.

quiz.q: If a = qb + r, why is gcd(a,b) = gcd(b,r)?
quiz.a: Common divisors of a,b are exactly common divisors of b,r because r = a − qb and a = qb + r.

quiz.q: Use the Euclidean algorithm to find gcd(48,18).
quiz.a: 48 = 2·18 + 12; 18 = 1·12 + 6; 12 = 2·6 + 0. The last nonzero remainder is 6, so gcd(48,18) = 6.

quiz.q: Suppose a|bc and gcd(a,b) = 1. Prove a|c using Bezout's theorem.
quiz.a: Bezout gives ax + by = 1. Multiply by c: acx + bcy = c. a divides acx and a divides bcy because a|bc, so a divides their sum c.

quiz.q: Why does the Euclidean algorithm always terminate?
quiz.a: Each remainder is a nonnegative integer strictly smaller than the previous divisor. A strictly decreasing sequence of nonnegative integers cannot be infinite, so a remainder 0 appears.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same gcd machinery drives RSA key generation, where large primes and modular inverses protect messages. Cryptographic libraries use fast primality tests such as Miller–Rabin and algorithms like Pollard's rho to find factors, because trial division is far too slow for 2048-bit numbers. Competitive programming uses extended gcd for modular inverse and linear Diophantine equations. Search next for 'extended Euclidean algorithm', 'modular inverse', 'Miller-Rabin' and 'RSA key generation'.
